scenarios.title: Restore useful denied-login detection
scenarios.summary: Repair a filter that detects denied logins without treating successful logins or unrelated messages as failures.
scenarios.objective: Match complete rejected-login records with a reported numeric IPv4 address for the supplied application. Handle the changing usernames, decimal ports and addresses in every supplied sample; do not restrict the filter to one recorded user. Leave accepted logins, unrelated applications, incomplete records and extra-text notices unmatched. Save the repaired virtual filter and preserve every supplied log sample.
steps: Inspect the example log and filter.
Edit, save and test the separate example.
Compare outcomes, diagnose a mistake and retry.

guide.title: 1. Read the records beside the example filter
guide.why: The starter’s accepted event word selects the wrong kind of login. The worked example shows how to describe a complete rejected record while allowing its fields to change.
guide.action: Read the workshop log lines and the event word in the example editor. Which lines describe rejected logins, and which describe successful or unrelated events?

commands.explanation: Read only the selected supplied virtual log sample.

guide.title: 2. Repair and test the saved example
guide.why: Expected: complete workshop rejected records match; accepted, incomplete, other-application and extra-text records stay unmatched. The command output and row labels show actual results after each run.
guide.action: Change the example event word from accepted to rejected. Save virtual filter, then Run command. Compare the actual labels beside each supplied line. Use Log sample to try the changed fields and lookalike events.

commands.explanation: Test the saved example filter against its selected virtual sample.

guide.title: 3. Diagnose a deliberate mistake and retry
guide.why: Successful logins become false positives and real failures are missed. Retrying uses the same preserved example; assignment work stays in its own editor.
guide.action: Use Check example. Then change rejected back to accepted in the example filter, save and run again. Read its failure feedback, restore rejected, save and check again.

scenarios.explanation: The repaired pattern selects this application’s rejected event, describes changing usernames and ports, and requires the reported address. Beginning/end anchors keep partial and extra-text records out. The saved filter is evaluated against contrasting samples rather than compared with one expected string; equivalent supported patterns can pass. This is offline classification, not a working protection daemon.
hints: Read one rejected and one accepted record. The fixed event word should describe the messages you need to detect.
Use the changing-field classes taught in the Introduction, and keep <HOST> as the complete reported-address field. Use ^ and $ to bound the required whole record.
Test the changing fields and lookalike samples too. A literal username misses other users; an unbounded or overbroad event pattern can select unrelated messages.
scenarios.simplifications: Offline fixed application messages and numeric IPv4 only. The disclosed common ASCII pattern subset excludes Python shorthand, lookarounds/backreferences, multiline/date processing, name lookup, includes and executable actions. This unit does not install/run Fail2ban, an IDS, a scanner or a firewall. Actual fail2ban-regex comparison is unavailable; fixed supported patterns were compared with Python re. All files, command output and changes are virtual.

scenarios.title: Remove health-check false positives without hiding real failures
scenarios.summary: Keep real denied logins detectable while excluding only explicitly marked failed health checks.
scenarios.objective: Match complete denied-login records for the supplied application, including changing names, ports and numeric addresses. Ignore denied records marked source=health; an interactive failure with the same username and address must still match. Leave accepted logins, unrelated notices and incomplete or extra-text records unmatched. Save the repaired virtual filter and preserve every supplied log sample.

Edit, save and test the separate example.
Compare outcomes, diagnose a mistake and retry.

guide.title: 1. Inspect the false positives beside the editor
guide.why: The starter selects successful events and ignores a username. The supplied health and interactive lines show why those are separate mistakes.
guide.action: Read the selected archive log sample and the example filter. Use Log sample to compare ordinary events with Health checks and real users sharing an identity. Identify the event word and source marker before editing.

commands.explanation: Read only the selected supplied virtual log sample.

guide.title: 2. Save a precise filter and test its real results
guide.why: Expected: genuine denied logins match, denied health checks are ignored, and successful logins remain unmatched. Actual results appear only after the test command runs.
guide.action: Restrict the example failure pattern to denied records, and make its ignore rule specific to denied source=health records. Save virtual filter, then Run command. Read each Matched, Ignored or Missed label beside the actual line.

commands.explanation: Test the saved example filter against its selected virtual sample.

guide.title: 3. Try a broader exception and repair it
guide.why: The interactive probe failure is now hidden as well. The failed sample explains the lost detection; restoring the specific exception repairs it.
guide.action: After Check example passes, change the ignore rule to select the probe username regardless of source. Save and test the health-exception sample, then Check example. Restore the narrow source marker and check again.

scenarios.explanation: The event-specific failure rule keeps accepted logins out. A separate narrow ignore rule identifies denied health checks by their source marker, while interactive failures sharing the identity remain detectable. All samples are checked again against the saved text. A passing filter test is not proof of an installed/running protection daemon or firewall action.
hints: Compare a denied health record with a denied interactive record that shares its username and address. What field distinguishes them?
The failure rule should identify the application and denied event, with ^ and $ bounding the complete record. The exception also needs the denied event and source=health.
A username-only or address-only exception is too broad. Accepted health records should remain unmatched because the stated exception is for denied health checks.

scenarios.title: Aim an alert at the protected upload service
scenarios.summary: Repair a reversed rule header and verify its protocol, address, port and direction scope.
scenarios.objective: Alert only on supplied TCP records from 203.0.113.0/24 to 192.0.2.40 port 8088 in that direction. Require the case-sensitive literal UPLOAD anywhere in the supplied payload; different client addresses and source ports must still work. Leave reverse traffic, out-of-subnet clients, other destination addresses or ports, UDP and lower-case or absent markers without an alert. Save the repaired virtual rule with a positive sid for this activity, and preserve all supplied records.

guide.title: Read the supplied pairs
guide.why: The starter has the endpoint pairs reversed; its arrow selects the response instead of the request.
guide.action: Compare the example rule with the supplied request and reverse records. Identify which endpoint sends the SYNC request and which receives it.

guide.title: Repair and replay the example
guide.why: Expected: only scoped TCP requests with the uppercase SYNC literal alert. Actual decisions appear beside records after replay.
guide.action: Put the example client network on the left and the receiving host and port on the right. Save virtual rule, then Replay record set. Use Record set to inspect endpoint and protocol contrasts.

guide.title: Investigate an overbroad repair
guide.why: Expected: the reverse response also alerts. Its failed case identifies the unwanted detection; restoring -> excludes it.
guide.action: Choose Check example. Then change -> to <>, save and replay Request and reverse direction. Read the false-positive feedback, restore ->, save and check again.

scenarios.explanation: The endpoint pairs select only the stated client network, receiving host and service port in the request direction. The literal content check then selects the marker. any in the source-port position permits changing client ports; <> would also admit the explicitly excluded response. Fresh contrasting records test those decisions rather than one command or rule string.
hints: Read source address and source port together, then destination address and destination port. Compare a request and its reverse record.
The -> arrow should follow the requested traffic direction. Keep the client port flexible while selecting the receiving service port.
Test every record set. A bidirectional or any-address repair can fix detection while introducing a false positive.
scenarios.simplifications: Bounded offline Snort3-style header and ASCII-literal subset over supplied decoded IPv4 records. No packet capture/decoding, TCP reassembly, stream or service buffers, flow state, regex, hex content, variable/list/range headers, real daemon, inline prevention or vulnerability scan. A local positive sid is required here for identification; upstream permits omission. No actual Snort comparison has been verified.

scenarios.title: Reduce marker alerts without losing required detections
scenarios.summary: Combine payload conditions and deliberate case handling, then test false positives and subnet boundaries.
scenarios.objective: Alert only on supplied TCP records from 10.24.32.0/20 to 192.0.2.60 port 8443. Require both the ADMIN marker, ignoring its letter case, and the exact case-sensitive literal action=reset anywhere in the same supplied payload; either order is allowed. Leave other actions, missing markers, out-of-subnet clients, wrong ports, UDP and reverse traffic without an alert. Save the repaired virtual rule with a positive sid for this activity, and preserve all supplied records.
steps: Add the missing condition and replay

guide.title: Compare actions beside the editor
guide.why: The starter checks only the marker, so a harmless action also alerts. The example requires both clues.
guide.action: Read Marker, required action and lookalikes. Compare the supplied AUDIT records with change=disable and change=view.

guide.title: Add the missing condition and replay
guide.why: Expected: both clues and the scoped endpoints are required; changed marker case still alerts. Actual results come from the saved rule.
guide.action: Keep the marker condition case-insensitive. Add a separate case-sensitive content condition for change=disable. Save virtual rule, then Replay record set. Use Record set to try Subnet edges and changing clients, then Content case, independent order and protocol.

guide.title: Test a case-handling mistake
guide.why: The uppercase action lookalike becomes an unwanted alert. Applying nocase to one content condition does not require applying it to every condition.
guide.action: Choose Check example. Add nocase to the action condition, save and replay Content case, independent order and protocol. Read its failed case, remove that modifier, save and check again.

scenarios.explanation: The header retains the required /20 client network and receiving service. The case-insensitive marker and case-sensitive action are separate required literals. Both must occur, but no relative cursor or ordering restriction was requested. Testing the harmless action, uppercase action lookalike and neighboring subnets detects broader rules that look plausible on one positive record.
hints: Compare an alert you need with the harmless action. What text distinguishes them after the marker?
Use a second positive content option so both the marker and required action must occur. Choose letter-case handling separately for each literal.
Check the just-outside /20 clients and uppercase action lookalike as well as the positive records; a rule that handles only one record is incomplete.

scenarios.summary: Repair the boot-file policy for BIOS and x64 UEFI clients without sending a boot file to ordinary DHCP clients.
scenarios.objective: Give each PXE client a compatible boot program using the supplied file inventory. Keep ordinary DHCP free of boot-file offers.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: An ordinary DHCP client can use its address lease immediately. A machine starting from the network also needs the address of a boot server and the name of a program on that server. A valid lease therefore says nothing about whether a boot file exists or can run.
guide.action: Read the introduction and worked example.

guide.action: Use Inspect a client, the virtual inventory and the appropriate configuration editor.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: Every listed client outcome must agree with the saved configuration.
guide.action: Save your edits and select Check configuration.

scenarios.explanation: The saved policy now selects a compatible program for each supplied architecture. The stored artifact type determines compatibility. The two clients can keep their leases while using different boot programs, and the ordinary client should never inherit an unconditional file.
hints: Choose each client under Inspect a client before changing the table.
The server address and relative filename identify a stored program together. Open Inspect boot server files to see its type.
If both PXE clients pass but the ordinary client still receives a file, inspect the unconditional offer.

scenarios.title: Connect to the iSCSI target that exposes the intended disk
scenarios.summary: Discover the virtual storage and connect to the export named in the inventory ticket.
scenarios.objective: Save a node record for the supplied target and portal. Connect to that export and verify the supplied LUN and disk WWN. Leave unintended sessions disconnected.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Read the failed requirement. Compare the saved record with the active session, and inspect the device identity or startup preview before checking again.

guide.title: Understand the task

scenarios.title: Repair the certificate chain for an HTTPS site
scenarios.summary: Use the supplied Apache configuration to restore trusted HTTPS for the reports site while keeping the archive site working.
scenarios.objective: Restore the reports site’s matching certificate name and trusted issuer path for the supplied client. Keep the archive client verifying its original site. Save and apply your configuration, then check both results.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Inspect the failing client and compare its requested name, selected host, certificate and issuer result.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: The first certificate in the configured file identifies the site and is called the leaf. Its listed DNS name must match the name the client intended to contact. The configured key must match the leaf’s public key.
guide.action: Read the worked example.

guide.title: Try the separate example
guide.why: The server can supply intermediate certificates after the leaf. A client uses those issuer links to reach an anchor it already trusts. Including a root in the server file cannot make the client trust that root.
guide.action: Use the separate client trials.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: Save configuration checks the file’s structure. Apply saved configuration checks the supplied file and key pair and updates the active listener. A successful apply can still leave a client unable to verify the name or build the issuer path.
guide.action: Check the saved and applied setup.

scenarios.explanation: Both clients reached their intended servers, matched their DNS names and built issuer paths to their own trust anchors. A matching key lets the listener use the certificate. A supplied intermediate completes the client’s issuer path.
hints: Compare Name to verify and Certificate served in the primary trial. Read the issuer message separately from the DNS name check.
Look for a supplied bundle whose first certificate identifies the reports site and whose next certificate supplies the missing issuer.
The key must match the first certificate’s public key ID. Apply the saved file before rechecking client trials.
scenarios.simplifications: One simulated Apache 2.4.8+ listener with literal names and supplied certificate and key IDs. Client trials use fixed trust anchors, day numbers, exact DNS names and known issuer links. No real files, credentials, browser, network, cryptography or server are used. The exercise omits certificate creation, protocol versions, wildcard names, alternate issuer paths, revocation, encrypted keys and real Apache reload behavior.
